archetype.name: Early Playoff Exit (run-prevention rebound)
archetype.definition: A division champion that turned a losing 2025 into 94 wins on pitching and defense, survived the Wild Card round, then went out in four NLDS games because the lineup stopped scoring.

report.headline: A pitching-led rebound to the East title, undone by eight NLDS runs

recap.finish: 94-68, first in the NL East; beat PHI 2-1 in the Wild Card Series, lost the NLDS 1-3 to LAD
recap.body:
This was a real comeback season, not a fluky one. A year after going 76-86 with a slightly negative run differential, Atlanta outscored opponents by 0.72 runs a game (5th in MLB) and won the East by six games over Philadelphia. The W vs Run Diff of +0.5 says the record matched the margin almost exactly. These 94 wins were earned, not borrowed from close games.

The turnaround came almost entirely from run prevention. Team OPS was .718, a point off 2025's .719 and only 16th in the league. But the staff ERA fell from 4.36 to 3.63 (5th), Def Rank jumped from 20th to 5th, and the fielders saved 11.7 runs. The bullpen earned an A+. Didier Fuentes (2.45 ERA, 31% K), Dylan Lee (2.14 FIP, 31 holds) and Raisel Iglesias (34 saves, 2.55 ERA) made late leads hold. Chris Sale was the rotation's anchor and one of the best starters in the league: 2.16 ERA, 200 strikeouts, 5.8 WAR.

The Hitters grade is an A, but that rests on a few players. Matt Olson (41 HR, 122 wRC+), Drake Baldwin (126 wRC+, 2nd among catchers) and Michael Harris II (121 wRC+, 4.5 WAR) did the heavy lifting. Ronald Acuña Jr. hit at a 120 wRC+ clip but played only 107 games. Two of the lineup's biggest workloads went the other way. Austin Riley (81 wRC+) and Ozzie Albies (86) took more than 1,300 plate appearances between them at below-average production, which is why a lineup with that many good bats ranked only 9th in scoring.

The season peaked early. Atlanta was 40-20 through May, outscoring teams by nearly two runs a game in April. Then June went 9-14, with the offense managing 77 runs in 23 games, about 3.3 per game. From June on the club played 54-48 ball. That was good enough to protect the cushion it had built, but it was not dominant: a 12-12 September and a 4-6 finish over the last ten games.

The postseason followed the same script. Atlanta took the Wild Card Series from Philadelphia, scoring 14 runs in three home games. Against the Dodgers it scored 3, 3, 1 and 1. The pitching held up: a 3.14 postseason ERA, and Tyler Mahle allowed two earned runs in 13.1 innings. Sale struck out 35% of hitters, and his FIP was well under his 4.26 ERA. The lineup's core went cold all at once: Baldwin hit .111, Olson .148 and Acuña .125. Harris (.407) and Albies (two homers) were the only real threats. Seven games is a small sample, but a team that couldn't afford a cold lineup got one at the worst time.

highlights.title: Bullpen as the backbone
highlights.body: The relief corps earned an A+, with three relievers ranked in the top 42 of 389 on the site. Their peripherals back it up: Lee's 2.14 FIP was better than his ERA, and Fuentes paired a 2.45 ERA with a 2.60 FIP. This is the most sustainable strength on the roster.

highlights.title: Sale's ace season
highlights.body: Sale's 2.16 ERA came with a 2.29 FIP, a 30.9% strikeout rate and a 4.8% walk rate. That is dominance, not good fortune. His 5.8 WAR was the most on the team by more than a full win, and he ranked 2nd of 215 starters.

highlights.title: A margin that matched the record
highlights.body: A top-five run differential paired with a near-zero W vs Run Diff means the 94 wins rested on outscoring people, not on close-game luck. That is a sharp reversal from 2025's 76-86.

lowlights.title: Lineup vanished against LA
lowlights.body: Eight runs in four NLDS games ended the season. Baldwin, Olson and Acuña combined for almost nothing at the plate, and the team's postseason OPS was .609. Over seven games that is mostly variance. Still, it exposed a lineup that leaned on a handful of bats.

lowlights.title: Riley and Albies dragged the offense
lowlights.body: Two everyday infielders finished well below average at the plate while taking 1,313 combined plate appearances. That gap kept a lineup graded A at 16th in OPS. Whether it lasts depends on whether these were down years, which the sheet can't settle.

lowlights.title: Rotation behind Sale ran on luck
lowlights.body: The rotation graded only a C, and its depth looked better on ERA than it really was. Holmes posted a 3.44 ERA against a 4.75 FIP, and Pérez a 3.04 ERA against a 4.32 FIP. Neither struck out even 18% of hitters, so expect those run totals to climb.

arc.note: A 40-20 start through May built the division lead. After a 9-14 June the club was merely good (54-48), splitting September and losing six of its last ten.

recap.nextYear: The foundation is the bullpen and Sale, and both look real by FIP. The lineup's production is concentrated in Olson, Baldwin and Harris, with Acuña a full-season boost if he plays more than 107 games. Riley and Albies are the clearest places to gain runs. The biggest warning sign is the back of the rotation: Holmes and Pérez beat their FIPs by roughly 1.3 runs each, and Elder and Mahle were league-average at best. So the staff's 3.63 ERA likely overstates its depth. There is little luck to give back in the record itself, since W vs Run Diff was +0.5. A repeat depends on starting pitching behind Sale and on two more league-average bats.

confidence.note: Full 162-game season; postseason conclusions rest on only seven games.
